bib.title: Controlled experiments on the web: survey and practical guide
bib.venue: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 18:140-181 (online 30 July 2008)

question: How should controlled experiments (A/B tests and generalisations) be designed, sized, implemented and run on the web, and what practical lessons did Microsoft/Amazon experimenters learn?
hypothesis: Controlled experiments give the best design for establishing causal links between changes and user behaviour, and building experimentation infrastructure has high ROI.
contributions: Sect. 3: review of web controlled experiments including statistical power, sample size and variance-reduction techniques, extensions and limitations
Sect. 4: alternatives to traditional MultiVariable Tests (concurrent and overlapping univariate tests)
Sect. 5: generalised architectures for experimentation systems; randomisation and hashing schemes that fail conditional independence tests
Sect. 6: practical lessons on analysis, trust and execution, culture

limits: Almost all numbers are worked examples or reported from talks and blogs (Amazon, Google, Microsoft Live Search, Eisenberg); no sample sizes, intervals or durations for most reported effects.
The hash and PRNG tests are described in two sentences each: no code, p-values, hash implementations or exact counts beyond 5 simulated experiments over 1M sequential IDs.

Sample size formula 16 sigma^2/Delta^2 assumes equal variants, 95% confidence, 80% power and a normal approximation; it ignores multiple-testing and sequential peeking (not discussed, and no stopping rules are given).

Authors concede: experiments give quantitative metrics but no explanations, measure only the experiment period, suffer primacy and newness effects, need implemented features, and consistency issues across devices (Sect. 3.6).
Interaction claims ('rare in practice') are experience, not measured; Sect. 6.2.2 says automatic abort is recommended, not that the authors report building one.

Dated: client-side vendors (Google Website Optimizer, Offermatica, Optimost) and 2008 platform details; no variance reduction beyond filtering (CUPED came later), no sequential or always-valid inference, no network interference treatment beyond the eBay item-randomisation example.
practices: Randomise by user (cookie ID) and keep each user's assignment consistent across visits (Sect. 3.1, 5.1).
Agree the OEC before the experiment, prefer a single metric or weighted combination, include long-term predictors such as lifetime value and repeat visits (Sect. 3.1, 3.2.4, 6.3.1).
Compute minimum sample size from power, effect and OEC variance estimated from an A/A test; avoid underpowered tests (Sect. 3.2, 6.2.3).
Reduce variance by using lower-variance OEC components and filtering to users exposed to the change (Sect. 3.2 point 3, 3.2.3, 5.3.1).
Filter robots that accept cookies and generate many actions (Sect. 3.4).
Ramp up treatment from 0.1% upward and automate abort on underperformance (Sect. 3.5.1, 6.2.2).
Run continuous A/A tests: check split percentages, data against system of record, 95% non-significant (Sect. 6.2.1).
Assign 50% of users to treatment for maximum power (Sect. 6.2.4).
Run for at least one to two weeks, then multiples of a week (Sect. 6.2.5).
Use a hash such as MD5 over user ID plus experiment ID for assignment; do not combine cached partial hashes by XOR (Sect. 5.1.2).
Do not launch 'no significant difference' features on the argument they do not hurt without checking power (Sect. 6.3.2).
Use experiments to test software migrations with the goal of retaining the null, with enough power (Sect. 3.5.3).
Randomise items, not users, when user-level randomisation interferes (eBay), is undesirable (price elasticity), or is impossible (SEO robots) (Appendix A).
Start with an A/B test; use concurrent or overlapping univariate tests rather than fractional factorial/Plackett-Burman designs for online MVT (Sect. 4).
Check that speed is not the reason a new feature loses (Sect. 6.1.2).
Compute the OEC for new users to guard against primacy and newness effects (Sect. 3.6 point 3).

terms.definition: A quantitative measure of the experiment’s objective.
Instead of an A/B test, you exercise the experimentation system, assigning users to one of two groups, but expose them to exactly the same experience.
The entity over which metrics are calculated before averaging over the entire experiment for each variant.
The probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis, H0, when it is false.
The probability of failing to reject (i.e., retaining) the null hypothesis when it is true.
Restricting the analysis to users, and to the portion of their behaviour, affected by the experiment.
